html:
My workstation runs a coding agent (opencode) on local models: a fast 30B-class model — Nemotron Lightning on an RTX 5090 — answers first, and a bigger GLM-5.3-Flash spanning two RTX PRO 6000s takes the turns the fast model can't. Between the agent and the engines sits a routing layer that decides, per request, which model serves. This post is the full account of getting that layer right: the architecture, the three bugs it hid, the experiments I ran to choose between five routing configurations, and the benchmark numbers behind every claim.

The three surfaces

The lab routes through three layers, each with a distinct job:

  1. LiteLLM (:4000) — the mandatory chokepoint. Auth, per-key spend tracking, a PII guardrail on outputs, and telemetry. Every call from every client passes through it; every model is an alias in its config.
  2. Switchyard server (:4010) — NVIDIA's routing server as a standalone container. It owns tier routing for clients that opt in via router-model aliases, and it exports rich Prometheus metrics.
  3. NeMo Relay gateway (:4040) — a host service whose in-process Switchyard plugin does the routing for opencode. The plugin emits its own OTLP metrics and traces, and — the property that matters — it can count and trace every call if the client names a route id instead of a plain model name. A plain name passes through uncounted by design: "this cannot capture traffic it was not configured for."

The two tiers on the routing layer:

tiermodelhardwarewire
weak / efficientNemotron Lightning 30B-A3BRTX 5090 (second box)OpenAI
strong / capableGLM-5.3-Flash2× RTX PRO 6000, vLLM TP2 (this box)Anthropic

What a routed request actually walks through

There are two shapes of route, and the difference is the whole story:

A passthrough route (direct-glm-local, direct-aitop-lightning, …) maps a route id to one model. No decision is made. Cost: ~0.04 ms measured. The only thing it buys is that the gateway counts and traces the call — which is exactly why my agent's default model is litellm/direct-glm-local rather than the plain alias.

A capability route (llm_classifier, mode = "capability") runs an LLM judge that estimates p_solve — the probability that the weak model completes the task — plus a capability boundary (supported / uncertain / unmatched). The policy is deterministic: p_solve ≥ threshold → weak tier; otherwise strong. And it fails closed: an invalid or unparseable verdict routes to the strong tier.

opencode ──> :4040 Relay plugin ──> capability judge (once per conversation)
                                     |  p_solve >= 0.7 -> Lightning
                                     |  else, or bad verdict -> GLM
                                     v
                    weak: Lightning (5090)   strong: GLM (2x PRO 6000)
                                     └──────────> LiteLLM :4000 ──> engine

The judge's frequency is itself configurable (classify_trigger): every request, every user turn, or once per session. With message_hash_fallback enabled, the session key is the first user message's text — so a normal conversation gets exactly one judge call and one tier decision for its whole lifetime, with no client-side session headers.

Bug 1: the dashboard that lied by being old

The first symptom was cosmetic: the Switchyard Grafana board read "Escalations: 0" while Prometheus clearly showed 100+ answers served by the capable tier. Nothing was broken — the dashboard's JSON was generated from the route config at generation time, and a route added that morning (auto-glm-aitop) postdated the last generation. The per-route tier panels read their tier pairs from routes.toml when the generator runs; a route added without re-running the generator is invisible to them.

Lesson one, and it generalizes: any artifact compiled from configuration has a staleness clock. The fix was mechanical (re-run the generator), but the failure mode — a dashboard confidently reporting a wrong zero — is the kind that gets built into decisions. The drift check now catches it.

Bug 2: the efficient tier that answered empty

This one was expensive because everything looked healthy. Tier counters said the efficient tier served its share of requests. Latency looked fine. Then I captured the actual answers, and every hard-task answer from Lightning was empty — all 500 completion tokens were thinking, zero characters of content.

The root cause chain:

  1. The gateway's answer targets spoke the Anthropic wire (anthropic_messages), because they were originally built for a Claude-Code-shaped client.
  2. LiteLLM's /v1/messages translation **drops chat_template_kwargs** — so the enable_thinking=false flag never reached the vLLM engine.
  3. Lightning thought with its default budget: ~220 tokens burned on "list three colors", the entire 500-token budget consumed on "write a fibonacci function" — thinking, no answer.

The fix was the same trick the routing judge already used: declare the same model id on an OpenAI-wire client (where the thinking flag survives) and point the route's weak tier at it. Before/after, measured on the same four hard tasks:

After the fix: 843–1960 characters of correct content per hard task (the fibonacci answer is correct; the code review catches the same NameError the big model catches), at 750–1100 ms — 2.5–4× faster than the big model. The efficient tier went from "answers empty" to "answers correctly, faster."

The general lesson: the wire format is behavior. The same model, same prompt, same flags — routed through a different provider API — thinks instead of answering. If you benchmark a tier, benchmark its answers, not its counters.

Bug 3: the judge with backwards polarity

With the wire fixed, the judge's conservative behavior stopped being dangerous — but it was still weird. Across every configuration, the judge escalated trivial one-liners ("What is 42?" went to GLM, deterministically, in every run) and kept all four hard tasks on Lightning.

The docs explain why: the packaged judge is a capability forecaster, not a difficulty scorer. It estimates whether the weak model can do the task, guided by a packaged capability-card rubric. For my stack that rubric is simply mismatched — and the proof is that swapping in a two-sentence custom rubric moved the escalation profile from 3/12 tasks to 7/12. The rubric is the product; the judge model is a commodity. (More on that in the experiments below.)

The experiment matrix

Once both bugs were fixed, I benchmarked five routing configurations on the same 12-task set (8 trivial, 4 hard), each task scored for which tier served it and how long it took. All non-live configurations ran on a throwaway gateway with probe routes — the live config was never touched mid-experiment.

configurationcapable / 12tasks escalated to GLMp50 latency
live: capability, packaged rubric, threshold 0.75ok, 42, reply-ok, year, snippet review196 / 56 ms
escalation mode (answer-first, confirmations=1)0none318 ms
capability + strict-completeness rubric6ok, 42, haiku, reply-ok, email, snippet310 / 421 ms
capability + neutral-simple rubric8ok, 42, summarize, colors, year, gpu-fib, bash, snippet282 / 374 ms
capability + GLM as the judge2reply-ok, year1602 / 2974 ms

Four findings worth the price of admission:

Escalation mode — answer-first — escalated nothing. The trajectory judge reads the completed weak answer and rules on whether the run is in trouble. Lightning's post-fix answers are good, so it declined all twelve turns. As routing that's a 200+ ms tax for zero tier changes — reject. As information it's a free, independent quality audit: a second judge reading actual outputs confirms the efficient tier's work.

A stronger judge did not fix the inversion. GLM-5.3-Flash as the judge escalated trivial prompts and kept the code tasks — same backwards profile, at 1.7 s per judge call. The defect is in the packaged rubric, not the judge model's intelligence.

The rubric moves the profile, crudely. A strict-completeness rubric ("multi-part requests, code that must run correctly, long structured output lower the estimate") was the first configuration to escalate hard tasks to the capable tier — at the cost of three wasted trivial escalations. The rubric is a prompt, so this knob is a prompt-engineering exercise with measurable consequences.

The judge is not deterministic run-to-run. The baseline's escalated-task set differed between morning and evening runs on borderline prompts. Any A/B conclusion smaller than ~2 tasks of difference is noise.

The thing I refused to believe — and the data that settled it

Every capability route I had seen judged every request. For an agentic workload where tool continuations pour in, that means judging the same opening task twenty times. I was sure this was wrong, and the v0.3.0 docs agreed: classify_trigger = "new_session" judges once and reuses the decision, and message_hash_fallback keys the session from the first user message when the client sends no session identity.

Measured on the live configuration — same twelve tasks, same opening texts, two repetitions:

Rep 2 reused rep 1's tier decisions with zero judge calls: p50 dropped from 82–3887 ms to 17–157 ms across the board (roughly 10×), with identical outputs. One judge call per conversation. That number is the difference between "routing as a feature" and "routing as a toll booth."

What shipped

The live configuration after all of this:

  • Route type llm_classifier, mode = "capability" — the judge estimates whether the fast model can do the task, with fail-closed semantics.
  • base_threshold = 0.7, threshold_step = 0.15 — quality-optimal: supported tasks need p_solve ≥ 0.7 to stay on the fast tier; uncertain tasks need ≥ 0.85; unmatched effectively always go to GLM. Concretely, the code-review-class task now escalates to GLM (its p_solve sits in the band the old 0.5 threshold let through), while the tasks Lightning provably answers correctly stay on the 5090.
  • message_hash_fallback = true + classify_trigger = "new_session" — one judge call per conversation.
  • The weak tier on the OpenAI wire — the fix that made its answers real.

End-to-end on the live route: once a conversation's decision is cached, trivial prompts come back in 17–70 ms; hard tasks that stay on Lightning complete in 1.0–1.5 s with full answers; the uncertain ones go to GLM. Every call counted, every call traced, spend attributed per client key.

The ledger I keep now

One more practice came out of this arc, and it is the least glamorous: a data-integrity ledger. Two of the benchmark runs happened while bugs were live, and their numbers had to be audited afterward — which measurements were contaminated (latency absolutes from the empty-answer era), which survived (judge decision profiles — the judge's own wire was healthy), and which artifacts were re-labeled as evidence rather than data. The dirty runs were deleted; the ledger in the notes says why, artifact by artifact. Debugging archives are not benchmarks.

What I would tell myself a week ago

  1. Generated artifacts have staleness clocks. If a dashboard is compiled from config, a config change silently orphans it until regeneration.
  2. The wire format is behavior. Thinking flags, reasoning budgets, and even whether the model answers at all depend on which provider API the proxy speaks upstream. Verify with real answers, not counters.
  3. Tier counters measure routing, not quality. "Efficient tier served the request" is true even when the answer is empty. Capture and grade content.
  4. Fail-closed judges change your cost curve. A judge that routes unparseable verdicts to the strong tier converts judge flakiness into spend. Bound it with timeout_ms.
  5. The rubric is the product. The judge model is interchangeable; the packaged capability-card rubric is where the routing policy actually lives. Treat it like a prompt you own, with its own eval set.
  6. Per-request judging is a choice, not a law. One judge call per conversation via session affinity — 10× on repeat turns — with a documented best-effort caveat: two sessions sharing an opening prompt share a decision.

The lab notes, the benchmark harness, the CSVs and the full data-integrity ledger live in my private lab repository, and every number above comes from those files. The console I watch this routing layer with is public: Nemo Console.
